output.brief: The remote promotion gap is mostly explained by time in level, not by where people work. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so 230 of 340 remote staff (68%) haven't reached the 18 months in level that the policy requires. Only 26% of office staff are in that position. Among people who are eligible, the rates are about the same: 20.0% remote against 21.1% office. Nomination and approval rates are also similar. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% against 11.6%). The gap shows up in every job family, but that doesn't point to a location effect, because the tenure mix is the likely cause there too. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Some proximity bias or uneven access to visible work, as the managers described, is possible but not shown. I'd advise against the three-day office rule. It targets a cause the data doesn't support, and it would hit about 180 staff who were hired on home-based contracts. Next, hold the proposal and report promotion rates only for eligible staff. Then re-check at FY2027, and look at who gets stretch assignments.
